Allyl isocyanide is CH₂=CH–CH₂–N≡C. Two rules do all the work:
**every bond, single or multiple, contains exactly one σ**; a double bond adds **1 π** and a
triple bond adds **2 π**.
**Count the σ bonds** by counting the links:
C1–H × 2 = 2
C1=C2 (the σ of the double bond) = 1
C2–H = 1
C2–C3 = 1
C3–H × 2 = 2
C3–N = 1
N≡C (the σ of the triple bond) = 1
Total = 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = **9 σ** ✓
**Count the π bonds:**
C1=C2 contributes **1 π**
N≡C contributes **2 π**
Total = **3 π** ✓
A quick check: the molecule is C₄H₅N with 5 hydrogens, and 5 C–H plus 4 heavy-atom links is
9 σ, which agrees.
Note that it is an **iso**cyanide: the carbon is attached to nitrogen, not the other way
round. The σ/π count comes out the same either way, which is why the question is safe to ask.
∴ 9 σ, 3 π.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|8|Pradeep Chemistry:
All four hydrides are **pyramidal**, so each has a net dipole; the question is which is
largest. The measured values fall sharply down the group:
NH₃ **1·47 D** ✓
PH₃ 0·58 D
AsH₃ 0·20 D
SbH₃ 0·12 D
Two effects work together, and both favour nitrogen.
**Electronegativity.** N is 3·0 against H's 2·1, a difference of 0·9, so each N–H bond is
strongly polarised towards nitrogen. P (2·1), As (2·0) and Sb (1·9) are no more
electronegative than hydrogen at all — in PH₃ the bond moment is almost nil, and lower down
the group it actually **reverses**, pointing towards hydrogen.
**Bond angle.** NH₃ has a bond angle of 107°, close to tetrahedral, so the three bond moments
reinforce one another along the axis. PH₃ (93·6°), AsH₃ (91·8°) and SbH₃ (91·3°) are nearly
right-angled, which makes the resultant much smaller, and their lone pair sits in an almost
pure s orbital contributing little.
So ammonia is the odd one out in its own group, which is also why it hydrogen-bonds and the
others do not.
∴ NH₃.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|9|Pradeep Chemistry:
A molecule has **zero** dipole moment when it is **symmetrical** enough for the individual
bond moments to cancel exactly. Test each hydrocarbon.
(b) **CH₃–C≡C–CH₃**, but-2-yne ✓
The molecule is linear about the triple bond with a methyl at each end. It has a **centre of
symmetry**: whatever lies on one side is matched exactly on the other, so the two C–CH₃ bond
moments point in opposite directions and cancel. μ = **0** — the lowest possible.
The others all have a resultant:
(a) **cis-but-2-ene** — the two methyls are on the **same** side of the double bond, so their
bond moments add rather than cancel. (The *trans* isomer would be non-polar; drawing it cis
is the point of the question.)
(c) **CH₃CH₂C≡CH**, but-1-yne — the two ends are different, an ethyl group against a hydrogen,
so nothing cancels. The ≡C–H bond is strongly polar because sp carbon is highly
electronegative.
(d) **CH₂=CH–C≡CH**, but-1-en-3-yne — again unsymmetrical, with sp and sp² carbons of
different electronegativity at the two ends.
∴ CH₃C≡CCH₃.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|10|Pradeep Chemistry:
The measured dipole moments are
NH₃ **1·47 D**, NF₃ **0·24 D**, BF₃ **0 D**
so the order is **NH₃ > NF₃ > BF₃** ✓
Each value needs its own explanation, and together they make this a favourite question.
**BF₃ = 0.** Boron has no lone pair, so BF₃ is **trigonal planar**. Three identical B–F bond
moments at 120° to one another sum to exactly zero, however polar each bond is on its own.
**NH₃ is large.** Nitrogen has a lone pair, so NH₃ is **pyramidal**. The three N–H bond
moments point towards nitrogen and have a resultant along the axis, and the **lone-pair moment
points the same way**. The two contributions **add**.
**NF₃ is tiny, though it is also pyramidal.** Fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen,
so each N–F bond moment points **away** from nitrogen — the opposite direction to the N–H
moments in ammonia. The lone-pair moment still points along the axis as before, so here the
two contributions **oppose** and nearly cancel, leaving only 0·24 D.
That NF₃ is almost non-polar despite having three of the most polar bonds available is the
real lesson of the question.
∴ NH₃ > NF₃ > BF₃.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|11|Pradeep Chemistry:
A molecule XF₃ can have **zero** dipole moment only if its shape is symmetrical enough for the
three X–F bond moments to cancel. Three identical bonds cancel exactly when they lie at 120°
in a plane — that is, when the molecule is **trigonal planar**, which requires the central atom
to have **no lone pair**.
Count the valence electrons for each candidate forming XF₃:
**(b) Boron** — 3 valence electrons, all three used in bonding, **no lone pair** ⇒ sp²,
**trigonal planar** ⇒ μ = **0** ✓
(c) Nitrogen — 5 valence electrons, three bonds and **one lone pair** ⇒ sp³, **pyramidal** ⇒
the bond moments do not cancel, and NF₃ has μ = 0·24 D ✗
(a) Chlorine and (d) bromine — 7 valence electrons, three bonds and **two lone pairs** ⇒
sp³d, **T-shaped**. ClF₃ is distinctly polar, μ ≈ 0·6 D ✗
So the zero dipole moment is itself the evidence: it tells you the central atom has used all
its valence electrons in bonding and has none left over, which among the options only boron
does.
∴ boron.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|12|Pradeep Chemistry:
Polarising power is the ability of a **cation** to distort the electron cloud of a neighbouring
anion. By **Fajans' rules** it increases with
small cation size, high positive charge, and a **non-noble-gas (pseudo noble gas)**
configuration.
Cd²⁺ and Ca²⁺ have the **same charge** and almost the **same radius** (Cd²⁺ 97 pm, Ca²⁺ 99 pm),
so neither of the first two factors can explain the difference. It must be the third:
**Ca²⁺** is [Ar] — a **noble gas** configuration, 2, 8, 8
**Cd²⁺** is [Kr]4d¹⁰ — a **pseudo noble gas** configuration, with **18 electrons** in the
outermost shell ✓
The eighteen-electron shell contains ten **d electrons**, and d orbitals are diffuse and shield
poorly. The nuclear charge is therefore felt much more strongly outside a Cd²⁺ ion than
outside a Ca²⁺ ion of the same size, and that unshielded pull distorts the anion.
The consequences are visible: CdCl₂ is far more covalent than CaCl₂, with a much lower melting
point, and CdS is coloured while CaS is white.
Options (a) and (b) are irrelevant — neither atomic number nor atomic mass governs polarising
power — and (c) is simply false, since the two ions are nearly the same size.
∴ option (d).
pradeep|Chemistry|0|13|Pradeep Chemistry:
By **Fajans' rules**, the polarising power of a cation rises with its **charge** and falls with
its **size**. The useful single measure is the **charge density**, charge ÷ radius.
The three cations are
Na⁺  charge +1, radius 95 pm
Mg²⁺ charge +2, radius 65 pm
Al³⁺ charge +3, radius 50 pm
The charge rises and the radius falls at the same time, so both effects push the same way and
the order is unambiguous:
Na⁺ **<** Mg²⁺ **<** Al³⁺
so **NaCl < MgCl₂ < AlCl₃** ✓
The radii shrink because all three ions are isoelectronic with neon — the same ten electrons
held by 11, 12 and 13 protons.
The chemistry follows the order exactly. NaCl is a high-melting ionic solid (801 °C); MgCl₂
melts at 714 °C; AlCl₃ is so covalent that it **sublimes** at 180 °C as the dimer Al₂Cl₆, and
dissolves in organic solvents. Al³⁺ distorts the chloride ion so strongly that the electron
pair is effectively shared.
∴ NaCl < MgCl₂ < AlCl₃.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|14|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
A molecule is **polar** when the bond moments do not cancel, and whether they cancel depends on
the **shape** — which depends on whether the central atom has a lone pair.
Take each one and count the lone pairs on the central atom.
**(a) BF₃** — B has 3 valence electrons, all bonded, **0 lone pairs** ⇒ **trigonal planar**.
The three bond moments at 120° cancel ⇒ **non-polar**
**(c) SiF₄** — Si has 4 valence electrons, all bonded, **0 lone pairs** ⇒ **tetrahedral**.
Four equivalent moments cancel ⇒ **non-polar**
**(d) XeF₄** — Xe has 8 valence electrons, 4 bonded, **2 lone pairs**. Those two lone pairs go
to opposite axial positions, leaving the four fluorines **square planar**. Opposite pairs
cancel ⇒ **non-polar**
**(b) SF₄** ✓ — S has 6 valence electrons, 4 bonded, **1 lone pair**. One lone pair in a
trigonal bipyramid gives the unsymmetrical **see-saw** shape. There is nothing to cancel the
lone pair's contribution or to balance the two axial bonds against the two equatorial ones,
so the moments leave a resultant ⇒ **polar**, μ ≈ 0·63 D
The pattern is worth remembering: among AXₙ species it is the **odd** number of lone pairs
that usually destroys the symmetry. XeF₄ has two and stays non-polar; SF₄ has one and does not.
∴ SF₄.

Note: the printed key gives (d). XeF₄ is square planar and its bond moments cancel exactly, so
it is non-polar; the key is wrong and has been corrected to (b).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|19|Pradeep Chemistry:
The electronegativity of a hybrid orbital depends on how much **s character** it has.
An s orbital is spherical and sits closer to the nucleus than a p orbital of the same shell,
so the more s character a hybrid has, the nearer the nucleus its electrons are held, and the
more electronegative the carbon behaves.
The s characters are
sp  = ½ = **50 %**
sp² = ⅓ = **33 %**
sp³ = ¼ = **25 %**
so the order of electronegativity is **sp > sp² > sp³** ✓
The effect is large enough to change chemistry, not just numbers.
**Acidity of terminal C–H:** ethyne (sp) has pKa 25, ethene (sp²) 44, ethane (sp³) 50. The sp
carbon holds the electron pair of the C–H bond so tightly that it will give up its proton to
a strong base, which is why sodium acetylide can be made and sodium ethylide cannot.
**Bond length:** the C–H bond shortens from 1·09 Å in ethane to 1·06 Å in ethyne, for the same
reason.
Options (a) and (c) each contain a reversal in the middle, and (b) has the order exactly
backwards.
∴ sp > sp² > sp³.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|23|Pradeep Chemistry:
A **regular** geometry is one in which all the positions round the central atom are equivalent,
which requires the central atom to carry **no lone pair**. A lone pair takes up more room than
a bond pair, squeezes the bond angles and makes the shape irregular.
Count the lone pairs on each central atom.
**(a) CHCl₃** — carbon has 4 valence electrons and forms 4 bonds. **No lone pair** ⇒ the four
positions are a regular **tetrahedron** ✓
**(b) PCl₃** — phosphorus has 5 valence electrons, 3 bonded, **1 lone pair** ⇒ **pyramidal**,
with the angle pushed down from 109·5° to about 100° ✗
**(c) XeF₆** — xenon has 8 valence electrons, 6 bonded, **1 lone pair** ⇒ a **distorted**
octahedron, the classic example of a lone pair spoiling an otherwise regular shape ✗
**(d) SF₄** — sulphur has 6 valence electrons, 4 bonded, **1 lone pair** ⇒ **see-saw**, the
least regular of the four ✗
So only CHCl₃ has a central atom with its full complement of bonds and nothing left over.
(Strictly the three Cl atoms and one H are not identical, so the angles differ by a degree or
two from 109·5°, but that is a difference in the substituents, not in the arrangement of
electron pairs, which is what the question is about.)
∴ CHCl₃.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|24|Pradeep Chemistry:
Use VSEPR. Count the electron pairs round iodine in **IF₇**.
Iodine has **7** valence electrons; each of the seven fluorines takes one to form a bond:
bond pairs = **7**, lone pairs = **0**, so **7 electron pairs** in all
Seven pairs with no lone pair among them arrange themselves as far apart as possible, and the
arrangement that achieves this is the **pentagonal bipyramid** ✓ — five fluorines in an
equatorial plane at 72° to each other, and two more along the axis at 90° to that plane.
The hybridisation is sp³d³.
The other shapes belong to other pair counts, which is the quick way to eliminate them:
(a) trigonal bipyramid — **5** pairs, as in PF₅
(b) octahedral — **6** pairs, as in SF₆
(d) square pyramid — 6 pairs of which **1** is a lone pair, as in BrF₅
IF₇ is the standard example of a seven-coordinate molecule, and it is slightly non-rigid: the
equatorial ring puckers and the fluorines exchange positions rapidly, because five atoms at
72° are somewhat crowded.
∴ pentagonal bipyramid.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|25|Pradeep Chemistry:
The measured bond angles are
NH₃ **107°**, PH₃ **93·6°**, H₂S **92·1°**, H₂Se **91°** ✓ smallest
Two trends combine to give this.
**Down a group the angle falls towards 90°.** In NH₃ the nitrogen is small and uses **sp³**
hybrid orbitals, giving an angle near the tetrahedral 109·5°, reduced to 107° by the lone
pair. As the central atom gets larger (P, then Se) its valence s and p orbitals differ more
in energy and hybridisation becomes negligible, so the central atom bonds through almost
**pure p orbitals** — and p orbitals are at **90°** to one another. The bonded atoms are also
further apart on a bigger central atom, so they repel each other less and there is nothing to
push the angle open.
**A second lone pair closes the angle further.** H₂Se has **two** lone pairs against PH₃'s one,
and lone pairs repel more strongly than bond pairs, so the two Se–H bonds are squeezed closer
together.
Selenium is both the largest central atom offered **and** carries two lone pairs, so both
effects point the same way.
∴ H₂Se.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|26|Pradeep Chemistry:
Work out each shape from the lone pairs on the central atom.
**SF₄** — S has 6 valence electrons, 4 used in bonding, so 2 left = **1 lone pair**. Five
electron pairs ⇒ trigonal bipyramidal arrangement; the lone pair takes an equatorial position
(where it is crowded by only two neighbours at 90° instead of three), leaving the **see-saw**
shape.
**CF₄** — C has 4 valence electrons, all 4 bonded, so **0 lone pairs**. Four pairs ⇒ a regular
**tetrahedron**.
**XeF₄** — Xe has 8 valence electrons, 4 bonded, so 4 left = **2 lone pairs**. Six electron
pairs ⇒ octahedral arrangement; the two lone pairs go **trans** to each other along the axis,
as far apart as possible, leaving the four fluorines **square planar**.
So the lone pairs are **1, 0 and 2** respectively, and because those numbers differ the three
shapes are **different** ✓
That rules out (a) and (b), which both claim the shapes are the same, and (c), which has the
lone-pair counts in the wrong order.
Notice that XeF₄, with two lone pairs, still ends up symmetrical and non-polar, while SF₄ with
one does not — an odd number of lone pairs is what destroys the symmetry.
∴ different with 1, 0 and 2 lone pairs respectively.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|31|Pradeep Chemistry:
Two species have the same geometry when they have the same number of **bond pairs** and the
same number of **lone pairs** on the central atom. Work each pair out.
**(d) SO₄²⁻ and ClO₄⁻** ✓
SO₄²⁻: 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs ⇒ **tetrahedral**
ClO₄⁻: 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs ⇒ **tetrahedral**
Same, and they are **isoelectronic** too — 32 valence electrons each.
Now the others:
**(a) CO₂ and SO₂** — CO₂ has 2 bond pairs and **0** lone pairs on carbon ⇒ **linear**, 180°.
SO₂ has 2 bond pairs and **1** lone pair on sulphur ⇒ **bent**, 119° ✗
**(b) NH₃ and BH₃** — NH₃ has 3 bond pairs and **1** lone pair ⇒ **pyramidal**. BH₃ has 3 bond
pairs and **0** lone pairs ⇒ **trigonal planar** ✗ This pair is the classic trap: the formulas
look alike and the shapes are not.
**(c) CO₃²⁻ and SO₃²⁻** — CO₃²⁻ has 3 bond pairs and **0** lone pairs ⇒ **trigonal planar**.
SO₃²⁻ has 3 bond pairs and **1** lone pair ⇒ **pyramidal** ✗ (SO₃, without the charge, would
have matched.)
∴ SO₄²⁻ and ClO₄⁻.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|32|Pradeep Chemistry:
**Isostructural** means same shape and same arrangement of electron pairs. Work out XeF₂ first.
**XeF₂** — Xe has 8 valence electrons, 2 used in bonding, leaving 6 = **3 lone pairs**.
Total 5 electron pairs ⇒ trigonal bipyramidal arrangement, sp³d. The three lone pairs take the
three **equatorial** positions, where they have most room, and the two fluorines are left
**axial** — so XeF₂ is **linear**, F–Xe–F = 180°, with 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs.
Now find the match.
**(b) ICl₂⁻** ✓ Iodine has 7 valence electrons, plus 1 for the negative charge = 8, exactly as
xenon. Two go into bonds, leaving **3 lone pairs**. Same count, same arrangement, same
**linear** shape. ICl₂⁻ is in fact **isoelectronic** with XeF₂, 22 valence electrons each.
The others:
(a) TeF₂ — Te has 6 valence electrons, 2 bonded, **2 lone pairs** ⇒ **bent**, like water ✗
(c) SbCl₃ — Sb has 5, 3 bonded, **1 lone pair** ⇒ **pyramidal** ✗
(d) BaCl₂ — an **ionic** solid, Ba²⁺ with two Cl⁻; in the vapour it is bent. Not a comparable
covalent species ✗
∴ ICl₂⁻.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|33|Pradeep Chemistry:
O₂F₂ has the same skeleton as hydrogen peroxide with F in place of H:
F–O–O–F  against  H–O–O–H
In both, each oxygen carries **two bond pairs and two lone pairs**, so each is **bent** at
about 109°, and the two halves are twisted out of the plane about the central O–O bond. The
result is the **open-book** (skew) structure: two planes meeting along the O–O bond at a
dihedral angle — 111° in H₂O₂ and 87° in O₂F₂.
So O₂F₂ is isostructural with **H₂O₂** ✓
The others do not have the O–O type skeleton at all:
(a) C₂F₂ is F–C≡C–F, **linear** ✗
(d) C₂H₂ is H–C≡C–H, **linear** ✗
(c) H₂F₂ would be the hydrogen fluoride dimer, held by a hydrogen bond, not a comparable
covalent molecule ✗
The twist is worth understanding: a planar arrangement would force the lone pairs on the two
oxygens to eclipse each other, and rotating about the O–O bond relieves that repulsion. It is
the reason neither molecule is flat.
∴ H₂O₂.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|41|Pradeep Chemistry:
Stability follows **bond order**, and bond order comes from the molecular-orbital electron
count. Start from O₂, which has 16 electrons, and add or remove.
O₂'s configuration ends ... σ2p² π2p⁴ π*2p², so
bond order = (bonding − antibonding) / 2
**O₂⁺** — 15 electrons, one **removed from the antibonding** π* ⇒ (10 − 5)/2 = **2·5**
**O₂** — 16 electrons ⇒ (10 − 6)/2 = **2·0**
**O₂⁻** — 17 electrons, one **added to** π* ⇒ (10 − 7)/2 = **1·5**
**O₂²⁻** — 18 electrons, two added to π* ⇒ (10 − 8)/2 = **1·0**
So the decreasing order is
**O₂⁺ > O₂ > O₂⁻ > O₂²⁻** ✓
The key point is that every electron added goes into an **antibonding** orbital, so each one
weakens the bond. The bond lengths confirm it exactly: 112, 121, 128 and 149 pm.
This is also why O₂⁺ exists as a stable cation in salts such as O₂⁺[PtF₆]⁻ — a discovery that
led directly to the first noble-gas compound, because the ionisation energy of O₂ is close to
that of xenon.
∴ O₂⁺ > O₂ > O₂⁻ > O₂²⁻.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|2|Pradeep Chemistry:
A **gem-dihalide** (Latin *geminus*, twin) has **both halogen atoms on the same carbon**. A
**vic-dihalide** has them on **adjacent** carbons. Check where the bromines sit in each option.
**(a) CH₃–CHBr₂** ✓ Both bromines are on **C-2**, the same carbon. This is 1,1-dibromoethane,
a **gem**-dihalide — and since the carbon carries two halogens and one hydrogen, it is also
called an **alkylidene** halide.
(b) BrCH₂–CH₂Br — one bromine on each of two adjacent carbons: 1,2-dibromoethane, a **vic**
(or alkylene) dihalide ✗
(c) CH₃–CHBr–CH₂Br — again adjacent carbons, 1,2-dibromopropane, **vic** ✗
(d) CH₃–CHBr–CH₂–CH₂Br — the bromines are on C-2 and C-4, separated by a carbon, so neither
gem nor vic ✗
The distinction matters chemically. A gem-dihalide on hydrolysis gives an **aldehyde or
ketone** (CH₃CHBr₂ ⟶ CH₃CHO), because two –OH groups on one carbon lose water; a vic-dihalide
gives a **diol** (BrCH₂CH₂Br ⟶ HOCH₂CH₂OH). That is the standard laboratory test.
∴ CH₃CHBr₂.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|2|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The first law is **ΔE = q + w**, with w the work done **on** the system. Apply it to each
process and see which statement does not follow.
**(a) Isothermal: q = −w** ✓ correct. For an ideal gas E depends only on temperature, so at
constant T, ΔE = 0 and therefore 0 = q + w, giving q = −w. Whatever heat goes in comes out as
work.
**(b) Cyclic: q = −w** ✓ correct. The system returns to its starting state, so ΔE = 0 because
E is a state function. Again q = −w.
**(c) Isochoric: ΔE = q** ✓ correct. At constant volume no expansion work is possible, so
w = −pΔV = 0 and ΔE = q. This is why a bomb calorimeter measures ΔE directly.
**(e) Expansion into vacuum: ΔE = q** ✓ correct. There is no opposing pressure, so
w = −p(ext)ΔV = 0 with p(ext) = 0, and ΔE = q.
**(d) Adiabatic: ΔE = −w** ✗ **incorrect**
Adiabatic means **q = 0**, so ΔE = 0 + w = **+w**, not −w. The sign is wrong. The physical
sense is clear: compress a gas adiabatically, work is done **on** it (w positive), no heat can
escape, so its internal energy and temperature must **rise** — ΔE must be positive when w is.
Writing ΔE = −w would say the gas cools when compressed, which is the opposite of what a
bicycle pump shows.
∴ statement (d).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|3|Pradeep Chemistry:
Start from the definition of the millimetre of mercury. One mmHg is the pressure exerted by a
column of mercury 1 mm high, so
p = h ρ g
with
h = 1 mm = 1 × 10⁻³ m
ρ = density of mercury = 13 600 kg m⁻³
g = 9·8 m s⁻²
Substituting,
p = (1 × 10⁻³)(13 600)(9·8)
= 13·6 × 9·8
= **133·3 N m⁻²** ✓
So 1 mmHg = 133·3 Pa.
A useful cross-check: standard atmospheric pressure is **760 mmHg = 101 325 N m⁻²**, and
101 325 ÷ 760 = 133·3 ✓ The same arithmetic run the other way.
That check also disposes of the distractors: 101·3 N m⁻² (a) is one **thousandth** of an
atmosphere in pascals, and 1013 N m⁻² (b) is a hundredth of it — both are atmosphere numbers
with the decimal point moved, not mmHg values. Option (d) is ten times too large.
The unit is also called the **torr**, after Torricelli, who built the first barometer.
∴ 133·3 N m⁻².

pradeep|Chemistry|0|4|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
**Specific heat** is the heat needed to raise the temperature of **one gram** (or one
kilogram) of a substance by one degree. Because it is already defined *per unit mass*, it does
not depend on how much of the substance there is: it is an **intensive** property.
So halving the volume of the gas — which, at constant temperature and pressure, means halving
the amount present — leaves the specific heat **unchanged** ✓
The test to apply is the one that separates the two kinds of property. Divide the system in
two:
**extensive** quantities halve — mass, volume, total heat capacity, enthalpy, entropy
**intensive** quantities do not — temperature, pressure, density, **specific heat**, molar
heat capacity
The distractors come from confusing specific heat with the **heat capacity** of the sample,
which *is* extensive and would indeed halve. The word 'specific' is precisely what makes the
difference, exactly as 'molar' does in molar heat capacity.
A useful way to see it: a cup of water and a bucket of water have the same specific heat,
4·18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹, but the bucket needs far more heat to warm by one degree because there is more
of it. The property per gram has not changed; only the number of grams has.
∴ remain constant.
